name: Whiplash-associated disorder
aka: neck strain after motor vehicle crash
populations: drivers and passengers in motor vehicle collisions
people with high initial pain, disability or post-traumatic stress (higher risk of slow recovery)
summary: Neck pain and related symptoms after a sudden acceleration-deceleration of the neck, usually a rear-end collision. The pain source is often uncertain. Many recover, but a substantial minority do not.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve over weeks to months (median self-reported recovery 59–108 days across arms of one grade I–II trial), but about 50% still report neck pain at 1 year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated whiplash-specific criteria. Needs pain-free active rotation, no neurological signs and near-normal Neck Disability Index scores

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Canadian C-spine rule first, to exclude fracture: sensitivity 99.4–100% in alert, stable trauma patients. Then classify by Quebec Task Force grade

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Used to exclude fracture or instability when the Canadian C-spine rule is positive; it does not usually identify the pain source

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults of all ages; age 35 or older and high initial disability predict slower recovery

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Varies substantially between countries; emergency department visits for WAD have risen over 30 years in the Western world

overview:
Whiplash-associated disorder (WAD) is the group of neck pain and related symptoms that follows a sudden acceleration-deceleration of the neck, most often in a rear-end motor vehicle collision. The Quebec Task Force graded it from 0 to IV by signs and symptoms [r1,r2]. It is common: emergency department visits for WAD have increased in the Western world over the past 30 years, and the annual cumulative incidence differs substantially between countries [r3].

The tissue source of the pain is usually uncertain. In selected people with chronic pain, double-blind controlled diagnostic blocks implicated the cervical zygapophysial (facet) joints in about half [r4,r5], yet routine imaging rarely shows a lesion that explains the symptoms (clinical observation). Many people improve over weeks to months, but about half still report neck pain at 1 year [r6]. Early pain intensity, disability, post-traumatic stress and fear of movement predict slower recovery, whereas few features of the collision itself do [r6,r7]. Care therefore centres on excluding serious injury, reassurance, advice to stay active, exercise, and early recognition of psychological and social barriers to recovery. No single intervention has been shown to be clearly superior [r2,r8].

epidemiology.text: A best-evidence synthesis of 32 scientifically admissible studies found that visits to emergency rooms for WAD have increased in the Western world over the past 30 years, and that the annual cumulative incidence differs substantially between countries [r3]. Younger age and female sex were associated with filing claims or seeking care for WAD, but the evidence was not consistent. Occupant seat position and collision direction were associated with WAD in one study. The authors concluded that evidence about risk factors is sparse, and seems to include personal, societal and environmental factors [r3].

intrinsic: Female sex and younger age: associated with claims or care-seeking for WAD, although the evidence is not consistent [r3]
Personal factors in general: the evidence for individual risk factors is sparse and needs better-designed studies [r3]
Once injured, older age (35 years or more), high initial Neck Disability Index and hyperarousal symptoms predict ongoing moderate or severe disability [r9]
extrinsic: Collision direction and occupant seat position were associated with WAD in one study [r3]
Head restraint and seat design (modifiable): preliminary evidence that head restraints and seats that limit head extension in rear-end collisions reduce WAD reports, especially in females [r3]
Insurance system: eliminating payments for pain and suffering was associated with fewer WAD claims in one study (a claims outcome, not an injury outcome) [r3]

mechanism.summary: WAD follows a rapid acceleration-deceleration of the neck, classically when a stationary or slow-moving car is struck from behind. The seat accelerates the trunk forward while the head lags behind, so the neck is driven into relative extension. The head then rebounds into flexion. In a sled study of ten healthy male volunteers (4 km/h) filmed with cineradiography, the neck did not extend as one smooth curve: C6 rotated backward first and C5 followed, while the upper segments went into flexion, giving an S-shaped neck with 'open-book' motion at C5–6 [r10].
sequence: The occupant sits upright, facing forward, with the head and neck in a neutral posture and the head restraint behind the head.
The car is struck from behind and accelerates forward. The seat back pushes the trunk forward within a fraction of a second.
The head, which has inertia, lags behind the trunk. The neck is forced to move from the lower segments upward [r10].
The lower cervical segments extend first while the upper segments flex, producing an S-shaped curve. The C5–6 segment shows an abnormal 'open-book' motion [r10].
The neck is then carried into overall extension, and the head is driven back toward the head restraint.
The head rebounds forward into flexion as the car and the occupant decelerate. The neck is restrained by muscles and ligaments, and by the seat belt at the trunk.
Pain and stiffness may start within minutes or be delayed by hours to days. Delayed onset of neck pain is common enough to be listed as a low-risk feature in the Canadian C-spine rule [r11].

variants.name: Frontal or side impact
variants.description: Collision direction was associated with WAD in one study, so the mechanism is not restricted to rear-end impacts [r3]. Frontal impacts drive the head into flexion first, then extension.

variants.name: Low-speed impact
variants.description: The S-shaped segmental motion was recorded in a 4 km/h sled test of healthy volunteers, which shows that characteristic neck motion occurs even at low speed [r10]. Collision speed and vehicle damage are poor guides to injury.

variants.name: Head rotated at impact
variants.description: A rotated head is commonly asked about because it loads one side of the neck. Few collision factors, such as impact direction and head restraint type, were prognostic in the best-evidence synthesis [r6].

variants.name: Non-vehicle acceleration-deceleration
variants.description: Sport collisions, falls and amusement rides can produce a similar mechanism. The same screening for fracture and cord injury applies.

anatomy.text: The cervical spine has a lordotic curve of seven vertebrae. The upper cervical segments (occiput to C2) provide about half of axial rotation. The lower segments (C3–C7) provide most flexion and extension. Each motion segment has an intervertebral disc anteriorly and a pair of zygapophysial (facet) joints posteriorly. The facet joints are oriented about 45° to the horizontal, have a capsule, and carry nociceptors. The C2–3 joint is supplied by the third occipital nerve, which is why it can refer pain to the head [r12]. The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, the ligamentum flavum and the ligamentum nuchae restrain motion. The deep neck flexors (longus colli and longus capitis) stabilise the lordosis, and the extensors (semispinalis, splenius, suboccipitals) and upper trapezius control the head.

structures.name: Zygapophysial (facet) joints and capsules
structures.role: Guide and limit segmental motion. They are a documented source of chronic neck pain after whiplash when diagnosed with controlled blocks [r4,r5].

structures.name: Intervertebral discs and longitudinal ligaments
structures.role: Anchor each segment and resist extension (anterior longitudinal ligament) and flexion (posterior longitudinal ligament)

structures.name: Deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis)
structures.role: Support the cervical lordosis and control segmental motion. They are trained by craniocervical flexion exercises.

structures.name: Neck extensors and upper trapezius
structures.role: Control the head and absorb load. They commonly guard (spasm) after injury.

structures.name: Third occipital nerve and greater occipital nerve
structures.role: Supply the C2–3 joint and the posterior scalp. They explain occipital headache arising from the upper neck [r12].

structures.name: Vertebral and internal carotid arteries
structures.role: Supply the brain. They can be injured by neck trauma and are screened for in the examination.

structures.name: Spinal cord and nerve roots
structures.role: Cord and root injury or compression are excluded when there are neurological signs (Quebec grade III)

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
No single lesion explains WAD. Candidate sources include the zygapophysial joints and their capsules, the discs, ligaments and muscles of the neck. For the zygapophysial joints there is controlled-block evidence: in 50 consecutive referred patients with chronic neck pain after whiplash, double-blind controlled blocks identified painful joints in 54% [r4]. In 68 patients, placebo-controlled blocks gave a prevalence of 60% (95% CI 46–73%) for C2–3 or lower cervical joint pain [r5]. These were selected, referred patients with chronic pain, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone with WAD. In most people the exact source cannot be identified with routine imaging or examination, and different structures probably contribute in different people. Fracture or dislocation is a separate, more severe category (Quebec grade IV) [r1].

Soon after injury, people who go on to a poor outcome show changes beyond the neck. In a prospective study of 76 people within 1 month of injury, all groups had local mechanical hyperalgesia in the cervical spine, but only people who still had moderate or severe symptoms at 6 months showed generalised hypersensitivity to all sensory tests. This suggests altered central pain processing [r13]. Psychological distress and acute post-traumatic stress also predicted poor outcome [r7]. Whiplash is therefore best understood as a combination of local tissue injury, nervous system sensitisation and psychological response.

structures.name: Zygapophysial joints and capsules
structures.effect: Proposed main pain generator. Controlled blocks implicated these joints in 54–60% of selected chronic patients [r4,r5]. Kinematic work suggests abnormal C5–6 motion in the S-shaped phase [r10].

structures.name: C2–3 joint and third occipital nerve
structures.effect: In 100 chronic whiplash patients, third occipital nerve headache (relieved by controlled nerve blocks) was found in 27% overall and 53% of those with dominant headache. Tenderness over the C2–3 joint was more common in those with a positive block [r12].

structures.name: Discs and ligaments
structures.effect: Anterior longitudinal ligament and annular strain are plausible in the extension phase but were not directly shown in the sources reviewed. Advanced imaging findings do not map reliably onto symptoms (clinical observation).

structures.name: Craniovertebral ligaments (transverse ligament, alar ligaments)
structures.effect: Rarely injured. Suspect them when there is upper cervical pain with instability symptoms or neurological signs, and image urgently (clinical convention).

structures.name: Vertebral and carotid arteries
structures.effect: Rare dissection with neurological signs is a red flag and is excluded before manual treatment (clinical convention).

muscles.name: Deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis)
muscles.effect: Motor function measures, including superficial flexor activity during craniocervical flexion, range of motion and kinaesthetic sense, were assessed early after injury. Loss of range of motion was associated with higher disability at 6 months [r7].

muscles.name: Upper trapezius, splenius, suboccipitals
muscles.effect: Protective guarding, tenderness and stiffness are common clinical findings (clinical observation). They are probably secondary rather than primary pain sources.

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers and thoracic extensors
muscles.effect: Disuse and altered posture can add load to the neck. Address them as part of rehabilitation (clinical convention).

cellular.description: Soft-tissue strain triggers bleeding, oedema and an inflammatory cell response, which causes pain, guarding and stiffness. Whiplash-specific healing times have not been established in the sources reviewed.
Fibroblasts and new capillaries lay down repair tissue. Pain and range of motion usually improve most in this period (typical clinical course).
Tissue strength and alignment improve with graded loading. Many people recover in this window; in one trial median time to self-reported recovery was 59–108 days across arms [r14].

A subgroup develops persistent pain with widespread hypersensitivity and psychological distress. This is linked to early sensitisation and post-traumatic stress, rather than to ongoing tissue damage alone [r13,r7].

systems.effect: Generalised hypersensitivity (including cold hyperalgesia) soon after injury marks people who do poorly, suggesting altered central pain processing [r13,r7].

Acute post-traumatic stress, psychological distress, passive coping, depressed mood and fear of movement predict slower or less complete recovery [r6,r7]. A physiotherapist-delivered stress-management program improved disability in high-risk acute WAD [r15].
A tendency to diminished sympathetic vasoconstrictor reactivity was seen in people with moderate or severe outcomes [r13,r7].
There is preliminary evidence that the prevailing compensation system is prognostic for recovery [r6]. Systems that remove payment for pain and suffering had fewer claims in one study [r3].
Neck stiffness and guarding alter posture, scapular control and thoracic mobility. These contribute to headache and arm symptoms (clinical observation).

grading.system: Quebec Task Force classification of WAD (grades 0–IV) [r1]

grades.description: No neck complaint and no physical signs [r2].
Neck complaint of pain, stiffness or tenderness only, with no physical signs [r1].
grades.prognosis: Usually the best prognosis, but early pain, disability and psychological factors still matter [r6]

grades.description: Neck complaint with musculoskeletal signs, such as reduced range of motion and point tenderness [r1].
grades.prognosis: Most people improve. High initial pain, older age and post-traumatic stress predict slower recovery [r9,r7]

grades.description: Neck complaint with neurological signs, such as reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes, weakness or sensory deficits [r1].
grades.prognosis: Needs neurological assessment and medical review; persisting deficits need specialist referral (clinical convention)

grades.description: Neck complaint with fracture or dislocation [r2].
grades.prognosis: Emergency management; not a physiotherapy-led condition

timeframes.summary: Recovery is variable. Many people improve over the first weeks to months, but about half still report neck pain at 1 year [r6]. Chronic WAD is conventionally defined as more than 3 months [r16]. The phases below are typical soft-tissue timeframes, not whiplash-specific healing times.

healing.description: Pain, stiffness and guarding are greatest. Priorities are exclusion of serious injury, reassurance and advice to stay active.
Pain and range of motion improve for most people. Early exercise and graded activity are introduced. This is the window to identify those at risk of a poor outcome [r9].
Strength, endurance and function are rebuilt. Median self-reported recovery in one trial was 59–108 days across arms [r14].
A subgroup have persisting pain and disability. Management shifts toward advice, active exercise and attention to psychological and social factors [r16,r8].

milestones.label: Fracture excluded; reassured and moving
milestones.note: Canadian C-spine rule applied at the first assessment [r11]

milestones.label: Active rotation restored toward normal
milestones.note: Typical clinical expectation in grade I–II; loss of range early predicts worse outcome [r7]

milestones.label: Primary outcome point in StressModex
milestones.note: Neck Disability Index mean difference −10 favouring stress inoculation plus exercise at 6 weeks [r15]

milestones.label: Chronic WAD threshold
milestones.note: Persisting symptoms beyond 3 months are classed as chronic [r16]

milestones.label: Median self-reported recovery
milestones.note: Median 59 to 108 days across arms in a grade I–II trial [r14]

milestones.label: About half still report neck pain

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not time-based. No validated return-to-sport criteria exist for WAD, so use pain-free active rotation, normal neurological examination, adequate neck strength and endurance, tolerance of sport-specific loading and psychological readiness. Contact and collision sport need full recovery first (clinical convention).

symptoms: Neck pain and stiffness, starting immediately or delayed by hours to days [r11]
Headache, usually occipital or suboccipital. In 100 chronic whiplash patients, 71 had headache with the neck pain [r12]
Shoulder, interscapular and arm pain or paraesthesia (arm symptoms suggest a root or plexus component and grade III screening)
Dizziness, visual or concentration disturbance, sleep disturbance and fatigue (clinical observation)
Post-traumatic stress features such as hyperarousal, flashbacks, fear of driving and worry about recovery. Hyperarousal predicts ongoing disability [r9,r7]
signs: Reduced and painful active cervical range of motion, especially rotation. Early loss of range predicts poorer outcome [r7]
Paraspinal and upper trapezius muscle tenderness and guarding
Local mechanical hyperalgesia over the cervical spine within 1 month of injury [r13]
Tenderness over the C2–3 joint in people with third occipital nerve headache [r12]
Normal neurological examination in grades I–II. Reduced reflexes, weakness or sensory loss place the person in grade III [r1]

subjective: Mechanism: direction and speed of impact, seating position, whether the head was rotated, and any head strike. Apply the Canadian C-spine rule before manual assessment [r11]
Onset: immediate or delayed pain. Delayed onset is a low-risk feature in the Canadian C-spine rule [r11]
Neurological symptoms: arm paraesthesia is a high-risk factor in the rule and prompts imaging [r11]. Ask also about balance, vision, swallowing and speech
Pain behaviour, headache, dizziness and function (driving, work, sleep)
Psychological and social factors: post-traumatic stress, fear of movement, coping style, mood, compensation and legal context [r6,r7]
Prior neck pain, previous injuries, comorbidities and medications
Patient expectations and goals, including whether they have been told to rest or wear a collar
observation: Head and neck posture; protective holding of the neck
Willingness to move the neck and willingness to turn to follow conversation
Bruising from a seat belt, signs of other injuries and general distress or hyperarousal
palpation: Midline cervical spine tenderness: bony midline tenderness requires imaging before further examination (Canadian C-spine rule) [r11]
Paraspinal, upper trapezius and suboccipital tenderness, and C2–3 joint tenderness [r12]
Local hyperalgesia (pressure pain thresholds) over the cervical spine in early WAD [r13]
rangeOfMotion: Active cervical rotation: in the Canadian C-spine rule, ability to actively rotate 45° to the left and right allows low-risk patients to proceed without radiography [r11]
Flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation, measured with an inclinometer or CROM device. Loss of range predicts poorer outcome [r7]
Assess thoracic and shoulder motion for contributing restrictions
strength: Craniocervical flexion test: control of the deep neck flexors with pressure biofeedback or by observation of superficial flexor substitution (a measure used in early WAD research [r7])
Neck flexor and extensor endurance (holding time)
neuro: Myotomes, dermatomes and deep tendon reflexes C5–T1 (grade III is defined by neurological signs [r1])
Brachial plexus provocation (upper limb tension) testing, which was used in early whiplash studies to assess neural mechanosensitivity [r7]
Upper motor neuron signs and gait, and cranial nerves where there are neurological symptoms, to exclude cord and cervical artery involvement
functional: Sitting, driving-posture tolerance and head turning for shoulder checks
Lifting, overhead reach and work tasks

specialTests.name: Canadian C-spine rule
specialTests.purpose: Decide who needs cervical radiography after trauma, in alert and stable patients (Glasgow Coma Scale 15)
specialTests.procedure: Step 1: any high-risk factor (age 65 or older, dangerous mechanism or paraesthesia in the extremities)? If yes, image. Step 2: any low-risk factor that allows safe assessment of range of motion (simple rear-end collision, sitting in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, or no midline tenderness)? If none, image. Step 3: able to actively rotate the neck 45° left and right? If not, image.
specialTests.positive: Any high-risk factor, no low-risk factor, or inability to rotate 45° each way: radiography is indicated.
specialTests.sensitivity: 100% (95% CI 98–100) in the derivation cohort; 99.4% in the later validation cohort
specialTests.specificity: 42.5% in the derivation cohort; 45.1% in the later validation cohort

specialTests.name: NEXUS low-risk criteria (comparator)
specialTests.purpose: An alternative decision rule for cervical radiography in trauma
specialTests.procedure: Applied by the physician before radiography. The criteria were compared head to head with the Canadian C-spine rule in 8283 alert, stable patients.
specialTests.positive: Failure to meet the low-risk criteria prompts radiography.

specialTests.name: Active cervical rotation to 45°
specialTests.purpose: Safe-screening step within the Canadian C-spine rule, and a baseline measure of range
specialTests.procedure: Seated patient actively rotates the head to each side. Do this only after the high-risk factors have been excluded.
specialTests.positive: Unable to rotate 45° to either side. This indicates imaging is needed in the rule.

specialTests.name: Palpation of the C2–3 joint
specialTests.purpose: Identify upper cervical joint involvement in headache after whiplash
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the C2–3 articular pillar posteriorly, comparing sides.
specialTests.positive: Tenderness over the C2–3 joint was significantly more likely in people whose headache was relieved by controlled third occipital nerve blocks (p = 0.01). No history or examination feature enabled definitive diagnosis without nerve blocks.

clinicalRules.name: Canadian C-spine rule
clinicalRules.description: Use first, in alert and stable trauma patients, to decide on radiography. It was 99.4% sensitive and 45.1% specific for clinically important cervical spine injury in a validation cohort of 8283 patients, and more sensitive than the NEXUS low-risk criteria [r11,r17].

clinicalRules.name: Whiplash clinical prediction rule (Ritchie)
clinicalRules.description: Full recovery was predicted by age under 35 years and initial Neck Disability Index of 32% or less. Ongoing moderate or severe disability was predicted by age 35 or older, initial Neck Disability Index of 40% or more and hyperarousal symptoms. In an external validation of 101 people, positive predictive values were 80.0% for full recovery and 90.9% for ongoing moderate/severe disability. It is a retrospective validation, and prospective validation is still needed [r9].

outcomeMeasures.name: Neck Disability Index (NDI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the StressModex trial, scored 0–100 [r15]. An NDI of 10% or less at 6 months defined full recovery in the prediction-rule validation [r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Numerical pain rating (0–10)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the PROMISE trial of chronic whiplash [r16]

outcomeMeasures.name: Global Rating of Change
outcomeMeasures.use: Patient-perceived recovery; a primary outcome in the Whiplash ImPaCT trial [r18]

outcomeMeasures.name: Post-traumatic stress and psychological distress screens (e.g. Impact of Event Scale, GHQ-28) and Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia
outcomeMeasures.use: Identify psychological risk factors for poor outcome, used in early whiplash prediction research [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: Cervical range of motion (inclinometer or CROM device)
outcomeMeasures.use: Track recovery; early loss of range predicts poorer outcome [r7]

imaging.indication: When the Canadian C-spine rule indicates imaging (high-risk factor, no low-risk factor or unable to rotate 45° each way) [r11]
imaging.findings: Fracture, dislocation or malalignment (Quebec grade IV [r2]). Imaging is often normal in grade I–II WAD (clinical observation).

imaging.indication: Neurological signs or symptoms, suspected ligamentous or cord injury, or red flags (clinical convention)
imaging.findings: Cord contusion, ligament disruption, disc injury or vertebral artery abnormality. Findings in people with only pain or stiffness rarely change management (clinical convention).

imaging.indication: Suspected cervical artery dissection: new severe neck pain or headache with neurological signs (clinical convention)
imaging.findings: Intimal flap, vessel narrowing or occlusion, intramural haematoma.

differentials.name: Cervical spine fracture or instability
differentials.distinguishing: High-risk mechanism, age 65 or older, midline bony tenderness, paraesthesia or inability to rotate 45°. Excluded first with the Canadian C-spine rule [r11].

differentials.name: Cervical arterial dysfunction (dissection)
differentials.distinguishing: New, severe, unfamiliar neck pain or headache with dizziness, visual disturbance, speech or swallowing difficulty or other neurological signs. Emergency referral.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Arm pain, paraesthesia or weakness in a root distribution, with positive neural provocation. Corresponds to Quebec grade III if neurological signs are present [r1].

differentials.name: Degenerative cervical myelopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Hand clumsiness, gait imbalance and upper motor neuron signs. Trauma can unmask cord compression in a stenotic canal.

differentials.name: Acute wry neck
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden painful loss of rotation with protective muscle spasm, usually without a collision. Pain is typically unilateral and settles over days.

differentials.name: Cervicogenic headache
differentials.distinguishing: Unilateral headache provoked by neck movement or posture. It can follow whiplash; third occipital nerve headache is a documented cause after whiplash [r12].

differentials.name: Concussion
differentials.distinguishing: Head strike or rapid head movement with cognitive, balance or visual symptoms. It can coexist with WAD, and symptoms overlap.

differentials.name: Thoracic outlet or brachial plexus injury
differentials.distinguishing: Arm symptoms provoked by arm elevation or plexus traction, with shoulder girdle tenderness and not a root pattern.

redFlags: Age 65 or older, a dangerous mechanism, paraesthesia in the extremities, midline bony tenderness or inability to actively rotate the neck 45° each way: cervical radiography is indicated before further manual assessment. Immobilise and send to the emergency department [r11].

Severe or progressive neurological deficit, such as limb weakness, bilateral paraesthesia, gait disturbance, bladder or bowel change or hand clumsiness: suspect cord injury or compression. Emergency referral.

New, severe, unfamiliar neck pain or headache with dizziness, visual disturbance, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, facial numbness or other neurological signs: suspect cervical artery dissection or stroke. Call an ambulance and do not manipulate the neck.

A sense of the head being unstable, severe guarding with pain on any movement, or pain with neurological symptoms on head movement: suspect upper cervical ligament injury or instability (for example the transverse ligament). Keep the neck still and arrange urgent imaging.
Fever, constant night pain, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer or immunosuppression: infection or malignancy is possible. Arrange urgent medical review.
Worsening symptoms, new neurological signs, or new psychological symptoms at any stage of care: refer for medical review. Persisting neurological signs beyond 3 months need specialist investigation.

management.principles: Begin by excluding fracture and serious injury with the Canadian C-spine rule and a neurological examination [r11]. After that, explain that the injury is common, usually improves and is not dangerous, and encourage normal activity. The evidence for any particular treatment is weak: a Cochrane review of 23 studies (2344 participants), eight of them of high quality, found that the evidence neither supported nor refuted either passive or active treatments for grade I–II WAD [r2]. In a 458-person trial, a rigid collar followed by mobilisation, advice to act as usual and an active mobilisation program produced similar outcomes at 1 year [r19]. In chronic WAD, a 20-session exercise program was no better than a single session of advice with telephone support [r16]. A clinical practice guideline suggests multimodal care for recent-onset grade III WAD, and supervised exercise with advice or advice alone for persistent grade I–II WAD [r8]. Because psychological factors predict recovery, screen for them and treat them early. A physiotherapist-delivered stress-management program added to exercise reduced disability more than exercise alone in high-risk acute WAD [r15]. Guideline-based care pathways have not clearly beaten usual care in recent trials [r18,r14]. Share decisions, set realistic expectations and review progress at each visit.

medical.name: Simple analgesia and short-course anti-inflammatory medication
medical.description: Paracetamol and short courses of oral NSAIDs, taken as directed by a doctor, to allow movement in the acute phase. Medication trials were not reviewed here, and the effect on long-term outcome is unknown.

medical.name: Cervical collar or prolonged rest
medical.description: A rigid collar followed by active mobilisation produced similar pain, disability and work outcomes at 1 year to advice to act as usual or an active mobilisation program, in 458 people within 10 days of injury [r19]. The Cochrane review also found no support for immobilisation [r2]. Collars are justified only for a suspected unstable injury, pending imaging.

medical.name: Specialist pain medicine: diagnostic zygapophysial or third occipital nerve blocks
medical.description: Controlled blocks identified painful zygapophysial joints in 54–60% of selected people with chronic neck pain after whiplash, and third occipital nerve headache in 27% [r4,r5,r12]. This supports referral of selected, persistent cases. Evidence for the denervation treatments that follow was not reviewed here.

medical.name: Psychological therapy referral
medical.description: For high post-traumatic stress, anxiety or depression. The effects of physiotherapist-delivered stress inoculation support integrating psychological care early; referral to a psychologist is appropriate when symptoms are severe [r15].

physio.name: Education, reassurance and advice to stay active
physio.description: Explain that recovery is usual, explain the uncertainty about pain source, encourage movement and normal activity, and teach self-management. Advice alone matched a 20-session comprehensive exercise program in chronic WAD (PROMISE, n = 172) [r16]. Act-as-usual advice performed similarly to collar or mobilisation in acute WAD [r19], and a guideline suggests advice alone for persistent grade I–II WAD [r8].

physio.name: Active exercise (range of motion, deep neck flexor, scapular and neck strengthening)
physio.description: Start early and progress by pain and function. A guideline suggests supervised exercise with advice for persistent grade I–II WAD and multimodal care for recent grade III WAD [r8]. However, evidence that exercise adds to advice is limited: in chronic WAD an intense program was not more effective than advice [r16], and a Cochrane review found inconsistent results [r2].

physio.name: Stress inoculation training integrated with exercise (high-risk acute WAD)
physio.description: A physiotherapist-led psychological component added to guideline-based exercise (10 sessions over 6 weeks) in 108 people with acute WAD, moderate disability and hyperarousal. Neck Disability Index mean difference favoured the combined program by −10 at 6 weeks, −7.8 at 6 months and −10.1 at 12 months [r15]. This is a single trial, and the training needs specific physiotherapist upskilling.

physio.name: Screening for prognostic factors (clinical prediction rule)
physio.description: Use age, initial Neck Disability Index and hyperarousal symptoms to flag people at risk of ongoing disability (positive predictive value 90.9%) [r9]. However, a risk-stratified clinical pathway in 216 people did not improve Neck Disability Index or global rating at 3 months [r18], so screening should prompt a conversation and tailored care, not a fixed pathway.

physio.name: Manual therapy (mobilisation or manipulation) as part of multimodal care
physio.description: Suggested within multimodal care in guidelines for recent-onset neck pain and WAD [r8]. The Cochrane review found inconsistent results for individual interventions [r2]. Avoid manipulation if any red flag, especially for cervical artery dysfunction, is present.

physio.name: Passive modalities alone (ultrasound, heat, electrotherapy, rest)
physio.description: The Cochrane review found that the evidence neither supports nor refutes passive treatments such as rest, immobilisation and ultrasound for grade I–II WAD [r2]. Use them only to enable movement, never as the sole treatment.

physio.name: Complete rest or prolonged avoidance of activity
physio.description: Act-as-usual advice and active mobilisation had similar results to immobilisation, so there is no evidence that rest improves outcome. Prolonged avoidance can feed fear of movement, which predicts slower recovery [r19,r6].

education: Whiplash is common and usually improves. Most of the improvement happens over the first weeks to months, but about half of people still have some neck pain at 1 year, so keep a plan going.
Hurt does not equal harm. The exact tissue source of the pain is often uncertain, and a normal scan does not mean the pain is not real.
Keep moving and return to normal activities (including work and driving) gradually. A collar and long rest do not speed recovery.
Stress, worry, poor sleep and fear of movement slow recovery, and they can be treated. Tell your physiotherapist if you feel on edge, have flashbacks or are avoiding driving.
See a doctor urgently for new weakness, numbness, severe headache with dizziness, vision or speech changes, or trouble walking.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and pain-guided. The first stage settles symptoms while keeping the person moving. The second restores range and deep neck flexor control. The third builds strength and endurance of the neck and shoulder girdle, and the fourth restores full function and manages persistent symptoms. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single trial. No single exercise program has been shown to beat advice in chronic WAD [r16], so choose exercises the person values and will do, and review at each visit. In high-risk people, add stress-management training [r15].

stages.name: Settle and stay moving
goals: Reassure and explain the likely course
Maintain normal daily activity and sleep
Identify risk factors for slow recovery
precautions: Exclude fracture and neurological signs first [r11]
Stop if arm symptoms, dizziness or neurological symptoms worsen
Avoid prolonged collar use and prolonged bed rest [r19]

exercises.name: Active cervical rotation, flexion and lateral flexion (sitting)
exercises.dosage: 10 slow repetitions each direction, every 1–2 hours while awake, within comfortable range
exercises.cues: Move to the first definite pain, then return. Breathe normally.

exercises.name: Craniocervical flexion (chin nod), supine
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions with 5–10 s holds, 1–2 times daily
exercises.cues: Nod as if saying yes. Keep the larger neck muscles relaxed.

exercises.name: Submaximal neck isometrics (sitting)
exercises.dosage: 5 holds of 5–10 s in each direction, at 20–30% effort, twice daily
exercises.cues: Press gently into the hand and hold. No head movement.

exercises.name: Walking and gentle activity
exercises.dosage: 10–20 min daily, building up as tolerated
exercises.cues: Swing the arms. Keep the head up and relaxed.

progressionCriteria: Pain at rest at or below 4/10 and settling
Active rotation improving toward 45° to each side or better
No new neurological symptoms and no red flags

stages.name: Restore range and deep neck flexor control
goals: Control of the deep neck flexors
Graded return to driving and work
precautions: Progress as symptoms allow; avoid provoking arm symptoms
Avoid repeated end-range loaded rotation in the first weeks

exercises.name: Craniocervical flexion with progressive holds (supine, then sitting)
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions with 10 s holds, once or twice daily; use pressure biofeedback if available
exercises.cues: Smooth nod without chin poking or jaw clenching.

exercises.name: Thoracic extension over a foam roller
exercises.cues: Support the head with the hands. Move through the upper back, not the neck.

exercises.name: Cat–camel
exercises.cues: Move the whole spine smoothly. Let the head follow the spine.

exercises.name: Neck isometrics progressed to 50% effort
exercises.dosage: 5 holds of 10 s in each direction, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Build effort gradually. Stay pain-free or mild.

exercises.name: Scapular setting and wall slides
exercises.cues: Lengthen the neck. Keep the shoulders away from the ears.

progressionCriteria: Active rotation and flexion near to the other side or the pre-injury range
Craniocervical flexion held for 10 s with minimal superficial muscle substitution
Pain at or below 3/10 with daily activities
Neck Disability Index falling over time [r15]

stages.name: Strength and endurance
goals: Neck and scapular strength and endurance
precautions: Progress load only if symptoms settle within 24 hours
Check for arm symptoms with loaded overhead exercises

exercises.name: Band or cable row
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down, with the neck long.

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–10 with a light load or body weight, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Lift the arms with the neck neutral. Stop before the neck takes over.

exercises.name: Resisted neck isometrics or band-resisted neck exercises
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–10, 2–3 times per week, progressing the resistance
exercises.cues: Smooth and controlled; avoid end-range loading early on.

exercises.name: Wall slides with a pause overhead
exercises.cues: Keep the ribs down and the neck relaxed.

exercises.name: Aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming)
exercises.cues: Keep moderate effort. It also helps sleep and mood.

progressionCriteria: Pain at or below 2/10 with loaded exercise and no next-day flare
Neck Disability Index approaching 10% or less, the full-recovery threshold used in the prediction study [r9]
Sustained sitting or driving for 30 min or more without symptom increase
Strength and endurance of neck flexors and extensors close to normal on endurance testing (clinical convention)

stages.name: Full function and persistent symptoms
goals: Return to all work, driving and recreation
Manage persistent symptoms with a self-management plan
Reduce fear of movement and hyperarousal
precautions: Persisting neurological signs need medical review
If symptoms are severe or stress is high, involve a psychologist [r15]

exercises.name: Graded exposure to feared activities (driving, head turning, sport)
exercises.dosage: Stepwise, 3–5 sessions per week, increasing exposure as anxiety settles
exercises.cues: Plan each step, rate worry and pain, and repeat until easy.

exercises.name: General strength training (upper limb, trunk and legs)
exercises.cues: Choose exercises the person enjoys and will continue.

exercises.name: Self-managed neck mobility and deep neck flexor maintenance
exercises.dosage: A short program, 3–4 times per week
exercises.cues: Use it as a flare-up plan. Return to activity quickly after a flare.

exercises.name: Stress management and sleep strategies
exercises.dosage: Daily practice, as taught by the physiotherapist or psychologist
exercises.cues: Breathing, pacing and sleep routines. Identify and plan for triggers [r15].

progressionCriteria: Neck Disability Index 10% or less, or a stable score the person accepts with a flare-up plan [r9]
Active rotation equal side to side with no provocation
Return to usual work, driving and recreation
Confidence and low fear of movement

criteria: No validated whiplash-specific return-to-sport criteria were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below are clinical convention
No red flags, and a normal neurological examination
Full or near-full active range of motion, with pain-free active rotation
Neck flexor and extensor endurance and shoulder girdle strength close to normal
Pain at or below 1–2/10 during sport-specific loading with no next-day flare
Neck Disability Index approaching 10% or less, the full-recovery threshold used in the prediction study [r9]
Psychological readiness, including confidence driving and playing, and agreement with coach and clinician
tests: Active cervical range of motion (inclinometer or CROM)
Craniocervical flexion test and neck flexor/extensor endurance tests
Sport-specific movement drills and contact-readiness assessment

prognosis: Prognosis is variable. A best-evidence synthesis estimated that approximately 50% of people with WAD report neck pain 1 year after injury, and that greater initial pain, more symptoms and greater initial disability predicted slower recovery [r6]. In a 458-person trial recruited within 10 days of injury, 48% reported considerable neck pain, 53% reported disability and 14% were still sick-listed at 1 year, irrespective of the early treatment [r19]. In grade I–II WAD, median time to self-reported recovery was 59–108 days across the three arms of one trial [r14]. Post-injury psychological factors, such as passive coping style, depressed mood and fear of movement, are prognostic for slower or less complete recovery. There is preliminary evidence that the compensation system is also prognostic [r6]. A prediction rule using age (35 years or over), initial Neck Disability Index and hyperarousal symptoms identified people with ongoing moderate or severe disability with a positive predictive value of 90.9% in external validation [r9]. Generalised hypersensitivity soon after injury marks a poorer course [r13]. Recurrence data were not identified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: Head restraint and seat design: preliminary evidence suggests head restraints and seats that limit head extension in rear-end collisions reduce WAD reports, especially in females [r3]. Advise correct head restraint height and distance as a practical measure (clinical convention).
Early identification and treatment of psychological risk factors (post-traumatic stress, fear of movement) may improve recovery in high-risk people [r15].
Early advice to stay active rather than rest or wear a collar [r19].
At policy level, removing payments for pain and suffering was associated with fewer claims in one study. This is a claims outcome and not a clinical prevention measure [r3].
clinicalPearls: Exclude fracture first. Apply the Canadian C-spine rule before any manual assessment: it was 99.4% sensitive in 8283 patients and more sensitive than the NEXUS low-risk criteria [r17].

Be honest about uncertainty. Controlled blocks implicate facet joints in about half of selected chronic cases, but most people cannot be given a precise structural diagnosis [r4,r5]. Say so, and focus on function.
Prognosis is shaped more by early pain, disability and psychological response than by collision severity [r6,r7]. Ask about worry, sleep and fear of driving on day one.
Generalised hypersensitivity early on (for example cold hyperalgesia) marks people who are less likely to recover. Check the whole body response, not just the neck [r13,r7].
Do not over-treat. A single session of advice matched 20 sessions of exercise in chronic WAD, so keep treatment proportionate and review often [r16].

Use the prediction rule to start a conversation about risk and to add psychological support for high-risk people, rather than to apply a fixed pathway. A risk-stratified pathway did not beat usual care in a trial [r9,r18].

captions.text: A driver waits at traffic lights with the neck in a neutral posture.
The car is hit from behind and accelerates forward. The seat pushes the trunk ahead.
The head lags behind, so the neck is forced into relative extension.
Then the head rebounds forward into flexion. The neck traces an S-shaped curve.
Pain and stiffness may start straight away or hours to days later.
Zooming into the neck, viewed from the side.

actions.text: A possible pain source: the facet joint

captions.text: The neck is a stack of vertebrae with a disc in front and paired facet joints behind.
In a collision the lower segments extend first while the upper segments flex.
The facet joint capsules and the front of the spine are loaded in this abnormal motion.
The deep neck flexors may be strained, and the muscles behind guard.
The facet joint is one proposed pain source, and the exact source is often uncertain.
Inflammation settles for most people, but a subgroup go on to have persistent pain.
A healthy facet joint capsule: aligned collagen with a thin, smooth synovial lining.
After injury, inflammation causes swelling and pain, and guards the joint.
With graded loading the tissue remodels, and most people recover. Schematic only.
